headline: Double Creek fluke on the drop, weakfish rebuild at the sedges, blues push into the Inlet mouth
subhead: Warm mid-70s bay water has fluke hugging the cool edges while bunker pods pull bluefish right up into Barnegat Inlet on the last of the incoming.
body_markdown:
I remember a July back in the late '80s, running a party of three out of Double Creek with the tide dead low and the air already sticky by seven in the morning, and my old captain — a Greek fisherman who'd taught me half of what I know, God rest him — told me something I've never forgotten. He said the bay doesn't hide from you in summer, it just makes you work for the cool water. Forty years later and that's exactly where we are right now. The shallow flats are running warm, mid-70s by midday, and every species worth chasing has tucked itself into the drop-offs and channel edges where there's a degree or two of relief and a little current to keep things moving.

Double Creek Channel has been my go-to the last ten days and it's holding up. The drift along the edge where it falls from six feet down into twelve to eighteen has been steady for fluke — nothing enormous, but a real dependable pick of keepers to about 22 inches, with the occasional better fish mixed in. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right along that break, has been the ticket, especially on the last two hours of the outgoing when the bait gets pulled off the flat and stacks up right on that lip. I've had my best drifts starting an hour before low and running through the turn — the fluke seem to sit tight to the channel wall waiting for that current to deliver breakfast, and a slow bucktail bounced right along bottom, tipped with a strip of squid, is about as close to a sure thing as this bay offers in July.

Now the weakfish — I'll be honest, I was cautiously optimistic about these fish rebuilding through the warm, calm evenings we've had, and that's exactly what's happened. The same sedge banks off Tices Shoal that were holding weakfish back in May and June are still producing, mostly at dusk and into the first hour of dark, on the calmest nights we've had. Small soft plastics — 4-inch chartreuse or pink shad bodies on light jigheads — worked slow along the edges of the grass has been drawing strikes from fish in the 16 to 20 inch range, with a few better ones mixed in for guys willing to stay out past sundown. It's not a blitz, and I want to be straight with you about that — you might make eight or ten casts before you connect — but the fact that these fish are showing consistently in the same water, week after week, tells me this isn't a fluke pattern, it's a real rebuild.

The bigger story this week has been bunker. Pods have been pushing through Barnegat Inlet on the higher stages of the tide, and where bunker go, bluefish follow. I've been working the inlet mouth — right around the rock jetty at Barnegat Light and out toward the sea buoy — on the last two hours of the incoming, and the blues have been all over those pods in broad daylight, which isn't something you see every week. Diamond jigs worked with a fast, erratic retrieve, or a simple bunker spoon trolled just outside the surf line, has been putting cocktail blues in the 2 to 4 pound range in the boat steadily, with the occasional bigger chopper mixed in when the pods get dense. If you're fishing from the beach at Island Beach State Park, this is the week to have a metal lip or a Hopkins in the bag — those bunker schools have been running close enough to shore that surf casters have gotten in on it too.

Striped bass remain the toughest read of the bunch, and that's typical for this time of year with water running warm right up into the mid-70s across the flats. The keeper-class fish have gone almost entirely nocturnal — best action has come after dark around bridge structure and current seams near Oyster Creek and up toward the Route 37 bridge, where a little current and some depth keep things bearable for a striper in July. Bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, or a fresh eel drifted slow along the pilings, has drawn a handful of solid fish in the 28 to 34 inch range for guys willing to fish the two hours around midnight tide changes. Daytime bass fishing in the bay right now is mostly a lost cause — I wouldn't waste your morning on it.

We're heading into the first-quarter moon on the 21st, which means the current is about to go slack for a few days — neap tides, less push through Double Creek and around the Inlet. That's typically when the fluke bite widens out a bit because the fish aren't pinned as tight to the strongest current lines, so don't be afraid to work the softer edges of the channel, not just the main thread. My read for the coming week: this pattern holds through late July as long as the weather stays settled and the bunker keep pushing through the Inlet. If a blow comes through and scatters that bait, the bluefish show could shut off fast at the Inlet mouth, so I'd get out there sooner rather than later if that's your target. Otherwise, Double Creek on the drop and the sedges at dusk remain the most honest bets on the bay this week.
